card.title: Centre of mass and centre of gravity

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The **centre of mass** $\vec r_{COM} = \sum m_i\vec r_i/\sum m_i$ is the point where a system's mass acts concentrated for translation; the **centre of gravity** is where the resultant weight acts (zero net gravitational torque). They coincide in a uniform gravitational field — all everyday cases — and separate only when g varies across the body, the COG then sitting slightly below the COM.…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **COM vs COG:** COM is mass-weighted position; COG is weight-torque-weighted position — identical only in a uniform g field.  ·  **COM can be empty space:** a ring's COM is at its hollow centre.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "The centre of gravity is the point at which the resultant weight of the body acts."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***2 kg + 6 kg at 2 m apart*** → COM 1.5 m from the 2 kg mass.

rows.text: No verified PYQ; NEB-style practice (definitions 2–3m, two-body numerical 3m).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Where an Object "Is" Every extended body behaves, under gravity and in collisions, as if all its mass were concentrated at one point. For most objects that point — the centre of mass — and the point where gravity effectively acts — the centre of gravity — coincide. Knowing where they sit explains balancing, stability and tumbling.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Centre of mass The **centre of mass (COM)** is the point where the total mass of a system may be assumed to be concentrated for translational motion: $$\vec r_{COM} = \frac{\sum m_i \vec r_i}{\sum m_i} \qquad \text{(continuous body: } \vec r_{COM} = \frac{1}{M}\int \vec r\, dm\text{)}$$ Two-particle shortcut: the COM divides the line joining $m_1, m_2$ in the ratio $m_2 : m_1$…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "COM divides the join in ratio m₂:m₁ — closer to heavier."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): Masses 1 kg, 2 kg, 3 kg sit at x = 0, 1, 2 m. Find the COM.** — x = (1×0 + 2×1 + 3×2)/6 = 8/6 = 1.33 m.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Most likely: the distinction question and a two-mass COM calculation.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **The whole body acts as a point mass at its COM** for translational motion and two-body orbits.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: $\vec r_{COM} = \sum m_i\vec r_i/\sum m_i$; COG = point of zero gravitational torque.  ·  They coincide when g is uniform; COG sits below COM for tall structures.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: High jumpers arch over the bar so their COM passes *under* it — less height needed for the same clearance.
